title: Behind the Explosion in Unconventional Education
author: Michael Horn
source: The Future of Education with Michael Horn (michaelbhorn.substack.com), August 17, 2026
summary: Michael Horn interviews Mickey Revenaugh, co-founder of Connections Academy, about her debut book School's Out: Why Families Are Choosing Unconventional Education, joined for the conversation by his own sixth-grade daughter Kayla. Revenaugh traces her research across the full landscape of unconventional schooling, Forest School, road schooling, unschooling, microschools, and virtual education, and argues the unifying thread is that children naturally love learning, but conventional schooling as constructed often extinguishes that instinct over successive grades. She offers a specific case study of an unschooler who was not an active reader until fourth grade, whose mother's willingness to trust the delay resulted in the child eventually earning a master's degree in social work, using it to argue that trusting a child's individual learning timeline does not foreclose academic achievement. On assessment, Revenaugh identifies portfolio assessment, evaluating a body of student-created work against a rubric rather than standardized test recall, as a decades-old idea she believes AI is now finally making practically feasible at scale, since AI can evaluate qualitative student output in ways that were previously too labor-intensive. She closes with an explicitly optimistic argument that the proliferation of unconventional models will ultimately be the best thing to happen to traditional school systems, forcing them to adapt to what families actually want as enrollment declines from falling birth rates and stalled immigration pressure districts to compete for students they might otherwise lose.
points: Identifies the unifying thread across radically different unconventional models (Forest School, road schooling, unschooling, microschools, virtual school) as the belief that children naturally love learning, and that conventional schooling as structured often extinguishes that instinct across the grades.

Offers a specific case study of an unschooler who wasn't an active reader until fourth grade, arguing that trusting a child's individual timeline, rather than intervening to correct a perceived delay, produced an adult who went on to earn a master's degree in social work.

Argues portfolio assessment, evaluating a body of student-created work against a rubric instead of standardized recall, is a decades-old idea from the 1990s that AI is now making practically feasible at scale by automating qualitative evaluation that was previously too labor-intensive.

Names three specific advantages unconventionally-educated kids carry into adulthood: retained love of learning, self-motivation without external prompting, and resilience/flexibility when an approach to a problem doesn't work on the first try.

Argues counterintuitively that unconventional education's growth will ultimately benefit traditional school systems by forcing them to adapt to falling enrollment driven by declining birth rates and stalled immigration, rather than threatening them.
quotes: One of the things that tied everything together for me was this idea that kids love to learn by their very nature and that school as we have constructed it often stamps that right out of them as they go through the grades.

One of the people I admire most in the unschooling world, was not an active reader until she was about in 4th grade. And it took a lot of courage for her and her mom to say, it's going to be okay. But that was kind of what it came down to, is that every kid's different, every kid deserves to learn the way that they learn best.

What I'm really excited about though is I think finally this will bring to fruition something that I've been excited about since the '90s, which is portfolio assessment. And by the way, AI gives us the tools to actually evaluate those things that we didn't before.

My personal theory is that kids who learn through really anything that's about something they're passionate about are going to be so much better off in the future that we're heading into than kids who have been traditionally taught.

I actually believe that all of these unconventional models are going to be the best thing that ever happened to traditional school systems because it's going to force them to adapt to what families and kids really want.
